title: Appeal Court overturns one of London officer's two convictions in woman's death
subtitle: Ontario's top court has quashed a London police officer's conviction for criminal negligence causing death in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman, but ruled a second conviction will stand.
article: The Ontario Court of Appeal has quashed a London police officer's conviction for criminal negligence causing death in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman, but ruled a second conviction will stand.

The case is headed to the Supreme Court because a lawyer for Const. Nicholas Doering said Friday his client has instructed him to seek leave from the country's highest court to review his conviction for failing to provide the necessaries of life that was upheld by the Appeal Court.

Doering was sentenced to 12 months in jail in 2020 after he was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in the Sept. 6, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn.
Doering, 31, was the first Canadian police officer to be convicted of the offence in an on-duty incident.

He arrested Chrisjohn, 39, in east London after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal methamphetamine. He transferred her to Elgin OPP custody on an outstanding arrest warrant, falsely telling OPP officers Chrisjohn had been medically assessed by paramedics, the court found.

Doering appealed his convictions during a one-day hearing in February, where his lawyer argued the trial judge, Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance, had formed the opinion Chrisjohn needed medical assistance, then interpreted the evidence through that lens, ignoring the opinions of multiple police officers experienced in dealing with intoxicated people.

In his decision released Friday, Ontario Court of Appeal Justice David Doherty acquitted Doering of criminal negligence causing death and upheld his conviction for failing to provide the necessaries of life.
Doherty ordered a new sentencing on the upheld conviction.

Doherty took issue with Pomerance's conclusion Doering deliberately misled OPP constables Mark McKillop and Ashleigh Billing when he transferred Chrisjohn to their custody and told them she'd been assessed by paramedics and her condition hadn't deteriorated.

Doering was relying on a conversation with Middlesex-London EMS supervisor Sean Hill, who looked at Chrisjohn through a police cruiser window after her arrest. Hill told Doering Chrisjohn's vitals would be "out of whack due to the drug" and he could take her to the hospital, but would end up waiting for hours while she was monitored.

"In my view, the trial judge's finding that the appellant deliberately lied to the OPP officers by indicating Ms. Chrisjohn had been assessed by EMS personnel as not requiring medical attention is unreasonable in the face of her contradictory finding that the appellant honestly and reasonably believed, that in Supervisor Hill's opinion, Ms. Chrisjohn did not need medical care," Doherty wrote in his decision.
"The Crown's case on the criminal negligence causing death charge loses considerable force when the alleged misrepresentation as to the assessment by EMS is removed from the evidentiary mix."
Doherty also highlighted Billing's "uncertainty" under cross-examination about what exactly Doering said.

"I cannot say that a trial judge would necessarily find that the appellant deliberately misrepresented Ms. Chrisjohn's condition based only on Const. Billing's evidence to the effect that the appellant told her that Ms. Chrisjohn had been in the same condition throughout the time he had custody of her."

Doering, who denied deliberately misleading the OPP officers, maintained his conduct was consistent with what a reasonable, prudent police officer would do and that it wasn't foreseeable that failing to provide Chrisjohn with medical attention would lead to her death.

But Doherty ruled Pomerance made no error in her analysis of Doering's liability on the charge of failing to provide the necessaries of life, saying the evidence showed a "reasonable, prudent officer" would have recognized the need for medical attention before transferring Chrisjohn to the OPP.
"That same reasonable, prudent police officer would also have been aware that Ms. Chrisjohn's life was endangered by the failure to seek medical advice and intervention," he wrote.

Doering's appeal lawyer, Alan Gold, applauded the decision to acquit his client on one charge. "We will be proceeding with the sentencing on the lesser offence of failing to provide necessaries as directed by the appeal court, but at the same time, we believe that this new conviction does contain legal error and I have been instructed to seek leave from the Supreme Court of Canada to review that conviction as well," Gold said by email Friday.
A lawyer representing the Chrisjohn family didn't respond immediately to a request for comment.
Doering has been suspended with pay since he was sentenced on Sept. 21, 2020, when he was taken into custody briefly before being granted bail after his appeal was filed.
